column4: The section reads 87:2’s خ ل ق and س و ي roots through bodily formation; 75:38 applies the same pair in sequence to a person who becomes an علقة.
The section distinguishes a fully formed from an unformed mudghah; 23:14 lays out the body’s progression through clot, tissue, bones, and flesh before another creation.
This ayah follows human life from dust and drop through infancy and maturity to old age, the same bodily course the section hears in the surah’s roots.
The section’s formed/unformed fetus and old-age stages meet here in مخلقة وغير مخلقة and أرذل العمر; the same ayah sets bodily formation beside dead earth swelling back to life.
The section traces formation inside the womb; 39:6 locates creation after creation in mothers’ wombs within three darknesses.
The section’s ق د ر root means setting things to a measure; this ayah joins what wombs decrease or increase to the claim that all things are with God by measure.
The section’s life course begins in the womb; this ayah explicitly names people as embryos in their mothers’ wombs and says God knows them from their earthly beginning.
The section’s womb-formed body has a close counterpart in this ayah’s secure lodging for the human fluid; the next ayat specify its term and measure.
The section describes stages before birth; this ayah says the fluid remains in that lodging until a known term, completing 77:21’s scene.
The section’s ق د ر root concerns a fitting measure; this ayah applies تقدير to that prenatal term and says the measure is excellent, after 77:22 names the term.
The section names a human life beginning before birth; this ayah recalls the drop of emitted fluid before the next ayah’s clot and formation.
The section itself points to this closing question: the One who formed the body from its beginning is able to bring the dead to life.
This ayah joins a mother’s pregnancy and delivery, nursing, full maturity, and age forty, spanning the bodily stages the section gathers into one life course.
The section’s measured-body image meets an ayah that names pregnancy, delivery, and allotted lifetimes, with each lifespan recorded.
The section hears creation and ordering as a human lifespan; this ayah says people were created in successive stages (أطوارًا).
The section’s خ ل ق and ق د ر roots are both applied to a human body here: a drop is created and measured.
The section treats creation and proportioning as bodily life stages; the speaker recalls being made from earth, then a drop, then formed as a man.
This is the section’s clearest bodily counterpart: God created the person, proportioned him, and balanced his form, using خ ل ق and س و ي.
The section’s formed-body image continues in this adjacent ayah: God assembled the person in whatever صورة He willed; this verse contributes the specific form chosen.
The section cites this ayah’s سواه and breathing of spirit as a bodily creation parallel to the womb-shaped person.
This ayah places the human drop in a secure lodging until an appointed term, giving a concrete prenatal interval for the section’s body stages.
This ayah begins after birth, when people are brought from their mothers’ wombs, and names the faculties given as they enter life beyond the section’s prenatal stages.
The section reads creation and proportioning bodily; this ayah says God created humans and then formed them, a direct human-form parallel.
The section explicitly joins the formed body to a drying pasture as two sides of one warning; this ayah depicts worldly life as watered growth that becomes scattered dry matter.
This ayah repeats the section’s growth-and-decay image: rain adorns the land with plants, then they are harvested and vanish, making visible what passes.
The section’s drying-pasture comparison recurs here as rain-fed growth that yellows and becomes debris, a second image of created life’s fading.
The section’s body begins in the womb; this passage begins its resurrection argument by reminding the denier that he was created from a drop.
After the human origin in 36:77, this ayah asks who can revive decayed bones, making the body’s later state the question answered by 36:79.
This ayah answers 36:78 that the One who produced the body the first time can revive it, the same creation-to-resurrection inference the section draws from 75:37–40.
The section’s prenatal beginning has a parallel in this ayah’s account of man being created from gushing fluid.
This ayah specifies where the fluid in 86:6 issues from; it makes the preceding creation claim bodily and anatomical.
After the fluid’s bodily origin in 86:6–7, this ayah states God can return the person to life, completing the creation-and-revival link.
The section cites س و ي in the dictionary sense of a man reaching the end of youth; this ayah uses واستوى of Moses after he reaches maturity.
This ayah says God shaped people and made their forms good, a concrete bodily use of the section’s formation roots.
The section’s image of a proportioned human body recurs in this ayah’s statement that God shaped people and perfected their forms.
The section’s creation-and-proportioning image meets this account of the human being formed and given spirit; the body is explicitly the object of the making.
This ayah likewise follows the human form being proportioned by the breathing of spirit, adding the embodied creation sequence that the section cites at 32:9.
In the same sequence that starts with a measured drop, this ayah says the person is made to die and buried, the life course’s bodily endpoint.
After death and burial in 80:21, this ayah says God will raise the person when He wills, completing the section’s creation-to-revival arc.
This opens a passage asking humans to consider their bodily origin; the next ayah identifies the fluid from which the person was created.
The section’s bodily course begins before birth; this ayah names human descendants as coming from an extract of fluid, leading into the proportioning in 32:9.
This precedes the section-cited 32:9 account: it says God perfected everything He created, introducing the human formation and spirit passage in 32:8–9.
The section’s formed-body image connects to the preceding announcement of a human being created from clay; the next ayah gives the forming and spirit-breathing detail.
This introduces the human creation sequence completed in 38:72, where proportioning and spirit-breathing make the bodily link explicit.
The section’s formed, sound body corresponds to this ayah’s statement that the human being was created in the best stature.
This opens the same account whose next verses trace the womb stages: human creation begins from an extract of clay, before descendants enter the secure lodging of 23:13.
After the developmental sequence in 23:12–14, this ayah says people die, extending the section’s body-through-life arc to its end.
This next ayah says people are raised after death, completing the life-cycle sequence begun with bodily formation in 23:12.
The section’s س و ي branch names the body at its youthful peak and its ك ب ر branch old age; this ayah explicitly reverses strength into weakness and gray hair.
The section’s ك ب ر branch names old age; this ayah says some are returned to the most decrepit age, reversing their earlier knowledge and strength.
This ayah makes aging a reversal of creation: whoever is granted long life is turned back in form, matching the section’s movement from bodily completion toward decline.
The section’s الدنيا branch links the present life to the passing bodily course; this ayah names people’s love of the immediate life.
This ayah says people leave the Hereafter, completing the contrast with the immediate life that the section’s الدنيا word helps stage.
The section connects preference for الدنيا to a human lifespan; this ayah says the transgressor prefers the life of this world.
This next ayah names Hell as the abode of the person who preferred worldly life, paralleling the section’s consequence for those who turn toward the present life.
Against 79:38’s preference for worldly life, this ayah describes the person who fears standing before God and restrains desire, the other response in the section’s warning.
This ayah names the Garden as the restrained person’s destination, completing 79:40’s contrast between the passing life and what endures.
The section pairs bodily formation and aging with pasture that withers; this ayah moves from pleased growth to yellowing debris and contrasts passing life with the Hereafter.
After the garden and dry-growth image in 18:45, this ayah distinguishes the passing adornments of worldly life from good deeds that remain.
After the best human form in 95:4, this ayah describes a fall to the lowest state; it can echo the section’s old-age decline, though the phrase is also read as a spiritual or afterlife lowering.
Zakariya says his wife is barren and he has reached extreme old age, a specific boundary to the section’s sequence from womb to aged body.
Zakariya likewise asks how he can have a boy when old age has reached him and his wife is barren, making conception at the far end of life a reversal.
The section’s الدنيا branch connects the present life to a passing lifespan; this ayah contrasts worldly enjoyment with what is better and more lasting with God.
This ayah calls worldly life play and amusement and the home of the Hereafter the real life, sharpening the section’s contrast between the present and lasting life.
After the fetus and revived earth in 22:5, this ayah states that God gives life to the dead; it makes the preceding bodily and soil images an argument for resurrection.
This ayah follows 22:5’s bodily stages by naming the coming Hour and resurrection from graves, the judgment that the prior life-and-earth images support.
This ayah asks whether humans were created from despised fluid; 77:21 then locates that fluid in a secure lodging, sharpening the prenatal scene.
This question introduces the bodily account in 80:19: the measured drop is the answer to “from what” the person was created.

The section follows life from the womb outward; in the sequence from a drop to death, this ayah says the way was made easy. The “way” may mean birth or the life course, so the bodily bridge is uncertain.
The section’s س و ي root describes a body set right; here the same root is applied to the human soul, extending proportioning from bodily form to inner capacity.
The section’s body-in-formation continues into maternal bearing and nursing here; the ayah names pregnancy’s weakness and two years of weaning.
The source section’s ر ب ب dictionary form is “to rear a child”; this ayah gives that growth a concrete duration by naming mothers’ nursing for two complete years.
The source section cites ر ب ب in the sense of raising a child; Pharaoh uses the matching verb نربك for having reared Moses as a child.
The source section’s ر ب ب dictionary branch is child-rearing; this prayer names parents’ having raised the speaker when small, giving that lexical sense a human scene.
The section follows human formation as a life stage; this ayah describes a spouse bearing a light burden that later grows heavier, a concrete pregnancy progression.
The source section’s د ن و dictionary branch describes a female camel nearing delivery; this ayah measures a pregnancy’s waiting term by childbirth, a specific near-birth parallel.
The section’s ك ب ر branch names aging; Zakariya describes weakened bones and gray hair while asking for a child, bringing old age and new life together.
This continues Zakariya’s old-age prayer from 19:4: he names his fear about those after him and his barren wife, giving the request for a child its bodily boundary.
The section’s ك ب ر dictionary sense is old age; this ayah names parents reaching old age while dependent on the child they raised.
After 40:67’s infancy-to-old-age sequence, this ayah says God gives life and causes death, extending that bodily chronology to its limit.
The section joins creating, proportioning, measuring, and guiding into a human-life image; Moses gives a parallel formula: God gave each thing its creation, then guided it.
This ayah says God created man from an علقة, the early body stage named in 75:38; it follows 96:1’s recitation command, whose root has the source section’s secondary womb sense.

The source section links the ق ر ء root to a dictionary sense of a womb closing over its young; this ayah uses اقرأ for recitation, and its next ayah creates man from a clot, so the association is indirect.
The section hears creation and proportioning as bodily formation; this ayah directly says God forms people in the wombs however He wills.
This repeated human-origin formulation begins with a mixed drop and continues to hearing and sight, connecting prenatal creation to the faculties with which a person enters life.
This ayah joins human creation from clay to an appointed term, a specific link between the section’s bodily origin and its measured life course.

The section’s womb sequence may connect with this ayah’s “resting place and deposit,” which some readings associate with womb and repository; the ayah itself does not specify those locations, so the parallel is uncertain.
